title: Electron-Deficient Bonding, Silicates and Inorganic Polymers
description: Boranes and Wade’s rules, three-center bonds, silicate minerals, zeolites, silicones and phosphazenes.
overview: The Lewis octet rule describes carbon, nitrogen and oxygen well, but the elements near boron and silicon need other ideas. Boron has fewer valence electrons than orbitals, and its hydrides are electron-deficient cages held by three-center bonds. Silicon, with no tendency to form π bonds, builds chains, sheets and frameworks of Si–O units, which make up more than 90% of the Earth’s crust.

This chapter covers the structure of the boranes and the electron-counting rules (Wade’s rules) that predict cluster shapes, the three-center bond in hypervalent molecules, the silicate minerals and zeolites, and inorganic polymers with Si–O and P–N backbones.
objectives: Describe the structure and bonding of diborane, including the 3c-2e bridge bond.
Apply Wade’s rules to classify a borane or carborane as closo, nido or arachno.
Describe the 3c-4e bond and explain hypervalent molecules without invoking d orbitals.
Classify silicates by the way SiO₄ tetrahedra link, and describe the structure and uses of zeolites.
Describe the synthesis and properties of silicones and polyphosphazenes.

sections.title: Boranes and three-center bonds
body: Boron has three valence electrons and four valence orbitals. A molecule such as BH₃ would have six electrons around boron, and it does not exist as such: it dimerizes. In **diborane**, B₂H₆, the two borons share a pair of hydrogen atoms in bridges, and the molecule has 12 valence electrons for eight B–H connections, so there are not enough electrons for eight 2-center bonds. Four terminal B–H bonds are ordinary 2c-2e bonds (8 electrons). The remaining 4 electrons hold the two bridging B–H–B units, each a **three-center two-electron (3c-2e) bond**: a single pair spread over B, H and B, formed by the overlap of two boron sp³ orbitals with a hydrogen 1s orbital. The B–H–B bonds are longer (1.33 Å) and weaker than the terminal B–H (1.19 Å) and the B–H–B angle is 83°. Such compounds are **electron-deficient**.

Lipscomb received the 1976 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the theory of boron hydride bonding. Diborane is prepared from NaBH₄ and BF₃ (3NaBH₄ + 4BF₃ → 2B₂H₆ + 3NaBF₄), ignites in air and is a strong Lewis acid and reducing agent. In THF it is the monomer adduct BH₃·THF, the reagent for hydroboration (see the chapter on alkenes). **Sodium borohydride** NaBH₄ contains the tetrahedral BH₄⁻ ion, a mild hydride donor and a common reducing agent (see the chapter on carbonyls).

sections.title: Higher boranes and Wade’s rules
body: Larger boranes are polyhedral cages (clusters). **Wade’s rules** classify their shapes by counting skeletal electrons, the electrons that hold the cluster together. Each B–H unit contributes **2** skeletal electrons (the three valence electrons of boron plus one from H, minus the two used for the B–H bond to hydrogen), each additional bridging H contributes **1**, and the charge adds electrons. The number of skeletal electron pairs, relative to the number of boron atoms n, gives the structure:

head: Skeletal electron pairs
Class
Shape
Example
rows: Closo shape with one vertex missing
Closo shape with two vertices missing
table.caption: Wade’s rules.

example.title: Applying Wade’s rules
solution: B₅H₉: five BH units give 10 electrons, and the four extra hydrogens add 4: total 14 electrons = 7 pairs. With n = 5, that is n + 2: **nido**, a square pyramid, the octahedron with one vertex removed.
[B₆H₆]²⁻: six BH units give 12, plus 2 from the charge: 14 electrons = 7 pairs = n + 1: **closo**, an octahedron.

body: **Carboranes** contain CH units in place of BH⁻ units. A BH unit supplies 2 skeletal electrons and a CH unit supplies 3. The icosahedral carboranes C₂B₁₀H₁₂ (the o-, m- and p-isomers) have 10 × 2 + 2 × 3 = 26 electrons = 13 pairs = n + 1, so they are closo, and very robust thermally and chemically. They have applications in boron neutron capture therapy for cancer, and as heat-resistant polymers. Wade’s rules extend to metal clusters and to transition-metal carbonyl clusters, which follow related electron-counting patterns.

check.q: A borane has 7 skeletal electron pairs and 5 boron atoms. It is…

check.a: A closed polyhedron with every vertex occupied
wrong: An open cage missing two vertices

sections.title: Hypervalency and three-center four-electron bonds
body: Molecules such as SF₆, PCl₅ and XeF₂ seem to have more than eight electrons around the central atom: they are **hypervalent**. The old explanation used d orbitals (sp³d², sp³d) but calculations show that d orbitals of main-group atoms are too high in energy and too diffuse to take part significantly. The better description is the **three-center four-electron (3c-4e) bond**, which accounts for hypervalency with only s and p orbitals.

Take F–Xe–F. The Xe 5p orbital along the axis combines with one p orbital on each F, giving three molecular orbitals: a bonding combination, a nonbonding one (located on the F atoms), and an antibonding one. The four electrons (two from Xe, one from each F) fill the bonding and nonbonding orbitals. The result is a bond order of ½ per Xe–F link, and a negative charge on the more electronegative F atoms. The same idea explains the axial bonds of PCl₅ and SF₄ (axial bonds are longer and weaker), the three halogens of I₃⁻ and the bonds in ClF₃. SF₆ can be described as three 3c-4e bonds along three perpendicular axes, using only the s and p orbitals of sulfur: its stability comes from the ionic character of the S–F bonds.

check.q: How does the 3c-4e bond explain hypervalency?
check.a: Four electrons occupy a bonding and a nonbonding MO spread over three atoms, using only s and p orbitals
wrong: It uses d orbitals on the central atom

sections.title: Silicates and zeolites
body: Silicon is bonded tetrahedrally to four oxygen atoms. The SiO₄⁴⁻ tetrahedron is the unit of the silicates, and the Si–O bond (452 kJ mol⁻¹) is very strong. Silicates are classified by how many oxygens each tetrahedron shares with neighbors:

head: Structure
Shared O per SiO₄
Formula unit
Examples
rows: Quartz, cristobalite; feldspars and zeolites when Al replaces some Si
table.caption: Silicate structures. More sharing of oxygens gives lower charge per silicon and a more extended structure.

body: When Al³⁺ replaces some Si⁴⁺ in a framework, the lattice carries a negative charge, balanced by cations (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺): these are **aluminosilicates**. The feldspars are the most abundant minerals in the crust. **Zeolites** are aluminosilicates with a framework with regular pores of molecular dimensions (0.3–1 nm). They act as **molecular sieves** (adsorbing water but excluding larger molecules, to dry solvents and gases), as ion exchangers (zeolite A softens water in detergents by trading Na⁺ for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺), and as acid catalysts in which the pores impose shape selectivity (ZSM-5 converts methanol to gasoline, and in catalytic cracking). **Glass** is amorphous silicate: sand (SiO₂) fused with Na₂CO₃ and CaCO₃ gives soda-lime glass, and adding B₂O₃ gives borosilicate glass (Pyrex), with a lower thermal expansion.

check.a: Framework silicate, with every oxygen shared between two silicons

check.q: What property of zeolites makes them useful as molecular sieves?
check.a: Their pores of fixed, molecular size

sections.title: Silicones and phosphazenes
body: **Silicones** (polysiloxanes) have an inorganic backbone of alternating silicon and oxygen atoms, –[R₂Si–O]ₙ–, with organic groups on silicon. They are made from dimethyldichlorosilane, (CH₃)₂SiCl₂, itself made by the Rochow direct process (Si + 2CH₃Cl, Cu catalyst, about 300 °C). Hydrolysis replaces the Si–Cl bonds with Si–OH, which condense with loss of water to chains and rings.

The Si–O–Si backbone is very flexible (the Si–O–Si angle is wide and the rotation barrier is low), so silicone polymers have glass transition temperatures near −120 °C, and stay fluid or rubbery over a huge temperature range (−50 to +250 °C). The Si–O bond is stronger than C–C, so silicones resist heat, light and oxidation, and the methyl groups make them water-repellent. Chain length and cross-linking give oils (lubricants, antifoams), greases, rubbers (sealants, gaskets, medical tubing) and resins (coatings).

A **phosphazene** has the repeating unit –N=PR₂–. Heating the cyclic trimer (NPCl₂)₃ to about 250 °C gives a high polymer, poly(dichlorophosphazene), (NPCl₂)ₙ, a rubbery material that hydrolyzes in moist air. The reactive P–Cl bonds can then be replaced by alkoxides, aryloxides or amines (OR, OCH₂CF₃, NHR), producing a family of stable polyphosphazenes with properties set by the side groups: flame-resistant elastomers, biodegradable polymers for drug delivery, and fuel-cell membranes. Like silicones, the backbone is very flexible and the properties are tunable, but the bonding in –N=P– is delocalized and better described as ionic (N⁻–P⁺) than as true double bonds.

check.q: Why do silicone polymers stay flexible at low temperature?
check.a: The Si–O–Si backbone rotates easily, giving a very low glass transition

quiz.q: How many of diborane’s 12 valence electrons occupy the two B–H–B bridge bonds?
quiz.why: The four terminal B–H bonds are 2c-2e bonds and use 8 electrons, leaving 4 for the two 3c-2e bridges (one pair each).

quiz.q: Why can BH₃ not be isolated as a stable monomer?
quiz.a: Boron has only six electrons and an empty orbital, so two BH₃ units share hydrogens
wrong: Three hydrogens cannot fit around such a small boron atom
The B–H bonds are too polar for three of them to bind one boron
It polymerizes at once through B=B double bonds
quiz.why: BH₃ is electron-deficient, with an empty p orbital on boron. Dimerization through 3c-2e B–H–B bridges relieves the deficiency.
Eight BH units give 16 electrons and the 2− charge adds 2: 18 electrons = 9 pairs = n + 1, a closo cluster.

quiz.q: An arachno borane cluster contains 6 boron atoms. How many skeletal electron pairs does it have?
quiz.why: Arachno clusters have n + 3 pairs, so 6 + 3 = 9. The values 7 and 8 correspond to closo and nido, and 10 to hypho.

quiz.q: A nido cluster of 6 boron atoms is built from a closo polyhedron with how many vertices?
quiz.why: Nido means a closo shape with one vertex missing. A 6-atom nido cage therefore comes from a 7-vertex closo polyhedron (compare B₅H₉, a square pyramid from an octahedron).

quiz.q: How many skeletal electrons does the carborane C₂B₄H₆ (two CH units and four BH units) have?
quiz.why: A CH unit supplies 3 and a BH unit 2: 2 × 3 + 4 × 2 = 14, or 7 pairs. With n = 6 that is n + 1, a closo octahedron. Counting every unit as 3 would give 18.

quiz.q: A student counts each BH unit as contributing 3 skeletal electrons because boron has 3 valence electrons. What is the error?
quiz.a: Boron’s 3 plus hydrogen’s 1, less the 2 used in the terminal B–H bond, leaves 2
wrong: Boron contributes only 2 electrons because it is in period 2
The terminal hydrogen contributes nothing, leaving 3 minus 1
Each BH unit contributes 1 because the cluster is electron-deficient
quiz.why: Of the 4 electrons available from B and H, a pair holds the exo B–H bond, so each BH unit leaves 2 for the cage.

quiz.q: In the 3c-4e description of F–Xe–F, what is the bond order of each Xe–F link?
quiz.why: Four electrons fill the bonding and nonbonding orbitals of the three-atom set, giving one bonding pair shared over two links: ½ each. The nonbonding pair sits on the fluorines.

quiz.q: Which prediction does the 3c-4e model make for the axial bonds of trigonal bipyramidal PCl₅?
quiz.a: They are longer and weaker than the equatorial bonds
wrong: They are shorter and stronger than the equatorial bonds
They are identical to the equatorial bonds
They are 2c-2e bonds, while the equatorial bonds are 3c-4e
quiz.why: The axial Cl–P–Cl unit forms a 3c-4e bond with bond order ½ per link, so those bonds are weaker and longer than the ordinary equatorial 2c-2e bonds.

quiz.q: Why is the d-orbital explanation of hypervalency no longer accepted for main-group atoms?
quiz.a: The d orbitals are too high in energy and too diffuse to take part significantly
wrong: The d orbitals are already filled, so they cannot accept electron pairs
The d orbitals are too small to overlap with ligand orbitals
SF₆ is purely ionic, S⁶⁺ with six F⁻, so there is no bonding to explain
quiz.why: Calculations show only a minor role for d orbitals. SF₆ has substantial ionic character, but the bonding is still described with s and p orbitals as 3c-4e bonds, not as an ion pair.

quiz.q: In a single-chain silicate each SiO₄ tetrahedron shares two corners. What is the anion per silicon?
quiz.why: Two unshared oxygens plus two shared oxygens counted as ½ each give 3 O per Si, and the charge is 4 − 6 = −2. SiO₄⁴⁻ is the isolated tetrahedron and Si₂O₅²⁻ the sheet.

quiz.q: A mineral splits easily into thin, flat flakes. Its silicate anion is most likely built from
quiz.a: tetrahedra sharing three corners in layers
wrong: tetrahedra sharing all four corners in a framework
quiz.why: Sheet silicates (micas, talc, clays) have strong bonding within layers and weak bonding between them, so they cleave into flakes. Double chains give fibers such as asbestos.

quiz.q: An aluminosilicate framework has the anion [(AlO₂)₄(SiO₂)₈]. How many Ca²⁺ ions balance its charge?
quiz.why: Each AlO₂ unit in place of SiO₂ adds one negative charge, so the framework is 4−. Each Ca²⁺ balances two charges, so 2 ions are needed.

quiz.q: How do the pores of ZSM-5 impose shape selectivity during acid catalysis?
quiz.a: Pore size decides which reactants can enter and which products can leave
wrong: The pores have a fixed negative charge that repels all organic molecules
The pores contain d orbitals that bind the reactant
The framework changes its Si–O bonds to match each substrate
quiz.why: The acid sites are inside channels of molecular dimensions, so only molecules that fit can react or diffuse out. This is the basis of the methanol-to-gasoline process.

quiz.q: How many moles of HCl are released when 5.0 mol of (CH₃)₂SiCl₂ hydrolyze and condense to silicone?
quiz.why: The equation n (CH₃)₂SiCl₂ + 2n H₂O → [–Si(CH₃)₂–O–]ₙ + 2n HCl releases two HCl per monomer, so 10 mol.

quiz.q: What best explains why silicones resist heat, light and oxidation better than hydrocarbon polymers?
quiz.a: The Si–O bond is stronger than C–C, and the backbone is already oxidized
wrong: Silicones are heavily cross-linked into rigid networks
Silicones are crystalline, and crystals do not oxidize
Silicones contain C=C double bonds that absorb light safely
quiz.why: The silicon–oxygen backbone is strong and cannot be oxidized further, and the methyl groups protect it. Silicones are flexible rubbers and oils, not rigid crystals.

quiz.q: Poly(dichlorophosphazene), (NPCl₂)ₙ, hydrolyzes in moist air. How is it turned into a stable polyphosphazene?
quiz.a: The reactive P–Cl bonds are replaced by alkoxide, aryloxide or amine groups
wrong: The N=P backbone is reduced to saturated N–P single bonds
The polymer is cross-linked through Si–O–P bridges
The chlorines are retained, and the polymer is stored under water
quiz.why: Substituting OR, OCH₂CF₃ or NHR groups for chlorine removes the hydrolytically labile P–Cl bonds. The side groups then set the polymer’s properties.

quiz.q: How is the bonding in the –N=P– backbone of a phosphazene best described?
quiz.a: Delocalized, closer to ionic (N⁻–P⁺) than to localized double bonds
wrong: Two localized N=P double bonds per repeat unit, as the formula suggests
Pure σ single bonds with no π component
Localized N≡P triple bonds alternating with P–N single bonds
quiz.why: The “double bond” notation is a convenience. As with Si–O, π overlap is poor, and the delocalized bonding resembles polarized N⁻–P⁺ links.

summary: Diborane has 3c-2e bridging B–H–B bonds. Compounds with fewer electrons than needed for 2c-2e bonding are electron-deficient.
Wade’s rules: skeletal electron pairs n + 1, n + 2, n + 3 give closo, nido, arachno clusters. A BH unit gives 2 skeletal electrons and a CH unit 3.
Hypervalent molecules such as XeF₂ and SF₆ are described by 3c-4e bonds, not by d-orbital hybridization.
Silicates are built from SiO₄ tetrahedra, classified from isolated units through chains and sheets to frameworks. Zeolites are porous aluminosilicates used as sieves, ion exchangers and catalysts.
Silicones have a flexible Si–O–Si backbone, a very low T_g and thermal stability. Polyphosphazenes have tunable side groups on an N=P backbone.

problems.q: Classify B₄H₁₀, B₁₀H₁₄ and [B₁₂H₁₂]²⁻ with Wade’s rules.
problems.solution: B₄H₁₀: 4 × 2 + 6 = 14 electrons, 7 pairs = n + 3: arachno. B₁₀H₁₄: 10 × 2 + 4 = 24 electrons, 12 pairs = n + 2: nido. [B₁₂H₁₂]²⁻: 12 × 2 + 2 = 26 electrons, 13 pairs = n + 1: closo (icosahedron).

problems.q: Explain why SiO₂ is a network solid while CO₂ is a gas.
problems.solution: Si–O single bonds are very strong (452 kJ mol⁻¹), and the Si=O π bond is weak because 3p–2p overlap is poor. Four single Si–O bonds are more stable than two Si=O double bonds, so silicon is surrounded by four oxygens in a network. Carbon forms strong C=O π bonds, so CO₂ is a small molecule.
problems.a: Strong Si–O σ bonds and weak Si=O π bonds.

problems.q: A zeolite has the formula Na₁₂[(AlO₂)₁₂(SiO₂)₁₂]·27H₂O (zeolite A). Why is it a water softener?
problems.solution: The framework has a negative charge from Al³⁺ replacing Si⁴⁺, balanced by mobile Na⁺ ions in the pores. Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ are held more strongly (higher charge density), so Na⁺ is exchanged for them, and the water is softened.
problems.a: Ion exchange of Na⁺ for Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.
